text.p: American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) in Brazilian telephone holding Telebras SA seesawed Wednesday on privatization and political news from Brazil.
In late morning Telebras, a bellwether for Latin American ADRs, were off 1-11/16 to 141-1/4. The ADRs were among the most-active issues on the New York Stock Exchange.

State-run Telebras had risen to an intraday high of 148-5/8, boosted by comments late Tuesday by Brazilian Communications Minister Sergio Motta that Brazil could complete the privatization of its telecom sector by mid-1998.

However, the ADRs then plunged amid reports the reformist government's lower house leader would resign because Motta had criticized government-allied parties in Congress. Traders awaited confirmation or denial of the report.

Ray Kelly, Latin American director at Robert Fleming, said the choppy trading reflected some investors' continued uncertainty about Latin American stocks. Equities in the region have been hit by jitters over a possible devaluation of the Brazilian currency, which analysts in Brazil largely dismiss.

The chance that lower house chief whip Luis Eduardo Magalhaes might resign "was a good enough reason to turn the market around," he said. "The spread (on Telebras) was $4 -- that gives an idea of the volatility on this thing."
Kelly added, "It will probably take a couple of weeks for this kind of volatility to go away."
Among other Latin American ADRs, Telefonos de Mexico was up 1/8 to 50-1/4 after the company reported mixed second-quarter results.
Several analysts reaffirmed their ratings on Telmex. Morgan Stanley Dean Witter analyst Luiz Carvalho raised his 12-month target price to $62 per ADR from $55.

Venezuelan telephone company CANTV was off 5/16 to 43-5/8. The drop came after the government barred CANTV and its competitor Telcel, 54 percent owned by BellSouth Corp, from signing up new subscribers amid widespread complaints about poor service and overbilling.
Paribas telecommunications analyst William Beavington reaffirmed his sell recommendation on CANTV.

Among other ADRs, Royal Dutch Petroleum Co fell 2/16 to 54-13/16 after Shell Oil Co, the U.S. subsidiary of Royal Dutch/Shell Transport, reported record second-quarter net income of $531 million. Analysts said the market had already priced in the better-than-expected results.
British news and information company Reuters Holdings Plc fell 1-3/4 to 60-1/2 after reporting half-year profits of 333 million pounds against forecasts of 335 million to 345 million pounds.
Advances led decliners 278 to 213 among 814 ADRs. The ADR group was up 0.45 percent and volume was 36 million ADRs.
